question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Place where the English East India Company received its Royal Charter in 1600]
options: London — Headquarters of the newly chartered East India Company
Greenwich — Location where Queen Elizabeth I signed the Charter of 1600
Lisbon — Capital from which the Portuguese controlled Eastern trade routes that the English sought to break
Amsterdam — Base of the Dutch merchants who competed with English traders in Asia
wrong_fact: Queen Elizabeth I did NOT sign the Charter of 1600 at Greenwich. The charter was granted in London; Greenwich is associated with the Royal Observatory but not the signing of the EIC charter.
explanation: The Charter of 1600 (formally 'The Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies') was granted by Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600. The charter was issued in London. Lisbon was indeed the hub of Portuguese Eastern trade empire that the English sought to rival, and Amsterdam was the base from which the Dutch VOC would later operate.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Key sea routes/regions mentioned in the Charter of 1600 granting English trade rights]
options: Cape of Good Hope — The southern tip of Africa that ships rounded to reach Asian waters
Strait of Magellan — An alternative westward route to Asia around South America
Persian Gulf — A key zone of English commercial interest in Asian trade from the start
Strait of Hormuz — Gateway to Persian Gulf trade, later a theatre of Anglo-Portuguese conflict
wrong_fact: The Persian Gulf was NOT a key zone of English commercial interest from the very start of the Charter of 1600. The initial focus was on the East Indies (spice islands) and India; Persian Gulf trade (via Surat and Gombroon/Bandar Abbas) developed later in the 1610s–1620s.
explanation: The Charter of 1600 covered trade 'beyond the Cape of Good Hope eastwards to the Straits of Magellan'. The primary early target was the spice trade of the East Indies (modern Indonesia). The Cape of Good Hope and Strait of Magellan were both noted as boundary markers. Persian Gulf and Hormuz trading posts came into prominence only after the Surat factory was established and Anglo-Portuguese rivalry developed in the 1610s.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Cities and their roles in the context of the English East India Company's Charter of 1600]
options: Goa — Principal Portuguese Estado da India headquarters that the English sought to bypass
Bantam (Banten) — First English trading post in the East Indies, visited by the initial EIC voyage
Calicut — The port on the Malabar Coast where the Portuguese had established their first Indian foothold under Vasco da Gama
Lisbon — City from where the EIC's first fleet under James Lancaster set sail in 1601
wrong_fact: The EIC's first fleet under James Lancaster did NOT sail from Lisbon. It set sail from Woolwich (on the Thames, near London) in February 1601. Lisbon was the Portuguese capital, not the EIC's departure point.
explanation: The Charter of 1600 authorised the EIC to trade. Goa was the Portuguese administrative capital in India. Bantam (Banten) in Java was indeed the destination of the first EIC voyage (1601–1603) under James Lancaster. Calicut (Kozhikode) was Vasco da Gama's landing point in 1498 and the Portuguese gateway to Indian spices. The first fleet sailed from Woolwich near London, NOT from Lisbon.
